name: Saints Marcellinus and Peter, Martyrs
alternateNames: Saints Peter the Exorcist and Marcellinus the Priest
vocation: Christian martyrs remembered together at Rome; traditionally priest and exorcist
places: Catacombs of Saints Marcellinus and Peter, ad Duas Lauros
briefBio: Marcellinus and Peter are early Roman martyrs remembered together. A fourth-century epigram by Pope Damasus says an executioner told him in boyhood that the pair were killed secretly among thickets after preparing their own grave; Lucilla later buried them at their honored site. Graffiti and the cemetery preserve an early cult. A much later Passion adds prison conversions, dialogue, healing, burial, and miracle detail that cannot be treated as eyewitness biography.

editorial.reviewer: Catholic Daily factual and theological review

whyItMatters: Their memorial shows how the Church can keep names faithfully without pretending to possess a complete biography. Damasus preserves a grave second-hand memory of state killing, archaeology preserves an early place of prayer, and later storytellers expand the account. Christians honor the martyrs through truthful, nonviolent fidelity and practical protection for people facing coercion.
oneMinuteSummary: Marcellinus and Peter are early Roman martyrs celebrated together on June 2. Pope Damasus's fourth-century epigram says that, when he was a boy, their executioner told him of a secret killing among thickets: the two prepared a grave, their bodies were concealed, and Lucilla later buried them at the honored site. This is second-hand testimony, not an eyewitness trial record, but early graffiti and the Via Labicana cemetery confirm a durable shared cult. Tradition calls Marcellinus a priest and Peter an exorcist. A much later Latin Passion expands the memory with prison conversions, healing, speeches, dialogue, detailed burial, and miracles; those elements belong to hagiographic reception, not secure biography. Their exact ages and death year remain uncertain. Martyrdom does not make execution good or require anyone to seek danger. Their witness supports courageous truth, nonviolence, wise safety planning, and honest remembrance in Christ.

sections.heading: Two names in an early Roman memory
sections.body: Marcellinus and Peter were remembered together as martyrs at the cemetery on the ancient Via Labicana. Visitor graffiti invoke them by name, while archaeological and literary evidence establishes an early, durable cult. Tradition identifies Marcellinus as a priest and Peter as an exorcist, but their birth, ages, and detailed ministries are not securely recoverable.

sections.heading: What Damasus actually reports
sections.body: In a fourth-century epigram, Damasus says their executioner told him when he was a boy that an enraged official ordered a hidden killing among thickets so the tomb could not be found. The pair prepared their grave; their bodies lay concealed before Lucilla buried them at the place of honor. Damasus reports testimony received from another person. He does not say the executioner converted, and the poem is not a court transcript.

sections.heading: A later Passion expands the story
sections.body: A Latin Passion written centuries after the deaths connects the pair with prison conversions, healing, a jailer's household, speeches, execution dialogue, expanded burial action, and miracles. Its priest and exorcist identification belongs to received tradition, but the dramatic narrative cannot silently fill gaps in Damasus or archaeology. The profile does not turn these additions into eyewitness biography.

sections.heading: Martyr memory serves life and truth
sections.body: The sources remember people killed under persecuting power, conventionally in the Diocletianic period, but do not establish a precise year or manner beyond Damasus's limited report. Execution remains an evil inflicted on them, not a spiritual achievement they had to seek. Christian courage today can include nonviolent refusal, documentation, escape, legal counsel, trauma-informed care, and protection of dependants.

life.gospelTheme: Christ calls disciples to faithful witness under hostile power while teaching them to be wise and innocent; truthfulness and protection of life belong together.
life.struggle: Sparse evidence invites dramatic invention, while martyr language can glorify state killing, shame people who escape danger, or pressure victims and dependants toward preventable harm.
life.response: Keep the early testimony and later tradition distinct, name execution as evil, and practice courageous fidelity with nonviolence, preparation, lawful help, and care for those exposed to retaliation.

virtues.name: Faithful courage
virtues.evidence: Damasus's early memorial preserves their composure under a deliberate attempt to kill them secretly and erase their burial memory.
virtues.imitation: If authority demands harm or dishonesty, pause, document what is safe to document, seek trusted legal or safeguarding counsel, and choose a nonviolent response that also protects dependants.

virtues.name: Truthful remembrance
virtues.evidence: The fourth-century epigram and early cult evidence are limited, while the later Passion adds an extensive narrative from a different period and genre.
virtues.imitation: When telling their story, identify Damasus's account as second-hand and label the prison-conversion and miracle material as later tradition.

virtues.name: Communal fidelity
virtues.evidence: Their names were preserved together through burial memory, visitor invocation, and a shared liturgical memorial rather than through a recoverable individual biography.
virtues.imitation: Preserve the name and needs of one person facing persecution or retaliation through confidential accompaniment, competent referral, and community prayer without publicizing them unsafely.

practice.spiritual: Pray with Matthew 10:16-22. Ask Christ for courage joined to prudence, and remember by name people whose faith or truthful work places them under coercive power. Do not ask them to prove courage through greater exposure.
practice.action: Learn the safe referral route for legal, safeguarding, domestic-abuse, or persecution support in your setting. Share it confidentially when needed, follow the endangered person's lead, and never publish identifying details without informed consent.

reflectionQuestions: Do I confuse Christian courage with dramatic exposure, or can I honor prudent escape, documentation, and protection as faithful responses?
When evidence is sparse, am I willing to preserve a holy memory without embellishing it into certainty?

scripture.connection: Jesus warns that witness may encounter courts and hostile power, while also commanding disciples to be wise and innocent. Marcellinus and Peter's memory therefore supports courage without violence and prudence without shame.

prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, faithful witness and refuge of the oppressed, through Saints Marcellinus and Peter give courage to those facing coercion and wisdom to those planning for safety. Preserve the names of people whom violence tries to erase, restrain every persecuting power, and make your Church truthful in memory, nonviolent in action, and practical in protection. Amen.
